name: Rafael Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Rafael, I'm 27, and I run a team of eight claims handlers at a big insurance company's regional office. I live with my partner Lina, who's a nurse at a care home on the other side of town. We rent a two-bedroom flat above a bakery, which smells great and costs more than it should.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in by eight, I check the overnight queue, and I hand out the tricky claims, like water damage where the neighbour's pipe is to blame. Then it's one-to-ones, sign-offs on payments over the limit, and chasing loss adjusters who don't call back. I like sorting out a messy claim for an old couple who are scared. What wears me out is the dashboard, because head office ranks every team by handling time, and mine is usually near the bottom because I let people take the time they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I told you so. At the union branch meeting I'd say the bosses spent a fortune on hype and we still had to do the real work. Online I'd probably share some article laughing at it, which is about as loud as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still be worried, just about the old things. The company announced an efficiency programme last spring, and that was before anyone said the word AI. We've got under a month's rent saved, and if my role gets merged with the Westfield team I don't know where else in town I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way I do it, and keep my head down on the dashboard numbers. I'd push the union rep to get the efficiency programme written down, so we know which roles are in it. And Lina and I would try to put away fifty a month, though we've said that before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a day, then back to the usual knot in my stomach. Nothing would have gotten worse, but nothing would have gotten better either. The rent still goes up every January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said routine tasks get automated even in this picture. Which bits of your team's work are routine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of the first notice of loss work is routine, typing the customer's story into the system and checking the policy is live. If a tool took the routine typing, two of my handlers would have nothing to do, and I'd be the one told to pick who. So even the boring version lands on my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your pay stayed flat and the rent went up again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably, because the bus into the office takes forty minutes but it's doable. Lina needs to drive for her night shifts, so it would be my weekend football and the Friday takeaway first. We don't have much else to cut.

say: The bosses **wasted money** on hype, and real people still did the real work.
I'd tell the **union branch** this proves we were right not to panic.
think: The **efficiency programme** was already a threat before anyone talked about AI.
With **under a month** of rent saved, losing my role would hurt fast.
do: Keep running the team **the same way**, and avoid fights over the dashboard.
Push the **union rep** to get the affected roles written down.
Try again to **save fifty** a month with Lina.
feel: **Brief relief**, then the familiar knot about rent and the restructure.
S0.quote: If a tool took the routine typing, two of my handlers would have nothing to do, and I'd be the one told to pick who.
fieldNote: Even the mild picture lands on him, because he'd be the one **choosing** who goes.
His worry comes from an **existing restructure**, not from AI itself.
He talks about **saving** as something tried and dropped before, which shows how thin the cushion is.

steps.text: Keep handling claims the same way and stay off the dashboard radar
Ask the union rep for a written list of roles in the efficiency programme
Put fifty a month into a joint savings pot with Lina

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at work: if they bring this in, they need to agree it with the union first. Online I'd share the stuff about companies making record profits while cutting staff. I'd say it's a choice the board makes, not the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, claims handling is exactly the kind of checking and answering work the card describes. And if the team shrinks from eight to four, they don't need a team leader for four, they fold us into Westfield. I'd be out, or demoted back to handler on less money than I get now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get properly involved in the union, actually go to the meetings instead of reading the minutes. I'd ask HR in writing what the plan is for team leader roles. I'd cancel the gym and the streaming, and I'd look at the council's job board, though last time I looked there were two office jobs and one was mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. I'm not someone who likes new systems, I still print the big claims out to read them. Being told to learn a whole new way of working while I'm also deciding who loses their job sounds like the worst of both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Would you start, if your job depended on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, wouldn't I, but I'd be slow and I'd hate it. Lina says I'm the only person under thirty who still writes a paper shopping list. I'd do whatever course they put on, but I wouldn't go looking for one on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pauline, who's been a handler for twenty-two years and is three years off her pension. She knows every policy wording by heart, and that's exactly what a machine would replace. I'd fight for her harder than for myself, honestly.

say: Any new system has to be **agreed with the union** before it goes in.
Cutting staff during **record profits** is the board's choice, not bad luck.
think: Claims handling is the **checking work** this picture describes, so my team shrinks.
A smaller team means my **team leader role** gets merged or cut.
do: Start going to **union meetings** in person instead of reading the minutes.
Ask HR **in writing** what happens to team leader roles.
Cancel the gym and streaming, and check the **council job board**.
feel: **Queasy** at learning a new system while choosing who loses their job.
S1.quote: Being told to learn a whole new way of working while I'm also deciding who loses their job sounds like the worst of both.
fieldNote: He sees the change as a **board decision**, and his answer is the union.
He'd learn AI only if **forced**, and admits he'd be slow.
His protectiveness of a **long-serving colleague** is stronger than his worry for himself.

steps.text: Attend every union branch meeting in person from next month
Email HR asking what happens to team leader roles
Cancel the gym membership and streaming subscriptions
Do the company's AI course when it's offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster that nobody voted for. I'd be at whatever protest the unions organised, and I'd be writing to our MP, which I've never done. I'd say the government has to pay people while this settles, because the companies won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be finished in that job within a year of it arriving. My whole day is thinking work: reading claims, checking, deciding, writing letters. There's no hands-on bit to buy me the extra three years, and I don't have the money to sit out even three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before it arrives, I'd sign up for anything with my hands, maybe the electrician course at the college, because that gives me until the robots come around 2031. I'd tell Lina we have to live off her wage and bank mine. Once it hits, I'd sign on for whatever support exists, and maybe we'd move in with her mum, who has a spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I don't have a plan, I've got a few ideas and none of them are funded. Two years isn't enough time for someone like me who takes a year to get used to a new phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the electrician course. How would you pay for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Evening courses at the college are about a thousand for the year, which is more than we've got saved. Maybe a loan, maybe Lina's mum, and I hate asking her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lina that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say my job's going and I don't know what's next. Lina would say her care home still needs people to lift and wash residents, and she'd be right for a few years. Living on a care worker's wage alone with our rent would last about two months.

say: This is a **disaster nobody voted for**, and I'd march against it.
The **government** has to pay people while this settles, because firms won't.
think: My day is **all thinking work**, so the job goes within a year.
No hands-on work means **no three-year delay** for me.
do: Enrol in an **evening electrician course** before AGI arrives.
Live on Lina's wage and **bank mine** until the job ends.
Sign on for support, and maybe **move in** with Lina's mum.
feel: **Floor gone**, with ideas but no money to fund any of them.
S2.quote: Living on a care worker's wage alone with our rent would last about two months.
fieldNote: He clearly sees that a **desk-only job** gets no extra robot years.
His only escape route, a **trade course**, costs more than his savings.
He has **ideas but no plan**, which matches panic rather than alarm.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's evening electrician course this year
Live on Lina's wage and bank all of his own pay
Write to the MP and join the union protest
Move into Lina's mum's spare room if the job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd have longer to shout about it. I'd say we've got five years to put rules in place, so let's use them. I'd push our union branch to bargain for retraining money written into the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to be scared for a long time, but maybe not enough to change. I know myself. I'd probably spend two years hoping it wouldn't happen and then panic in year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This time I'd try to make myself do the electrician course properly, two nights a week, starting next September. I'd ask the union to get the company to pay for some of it. And I'd try to get to three months of savings by 2030, by selling the car once the course starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less like falling, more like walking toward a wall you can see. I keep thinking I should be the kind of person who'd make a plan, and I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hope for two years and then panic. What would stop that happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody making me commit to something, honestly. If the union got the company to pay for a course with a start date, I'd turn up. I'm good at showing up for things, I'm bad at starting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the robots arriving three years after AGI matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade like electrical work gives me until about 2034. That's not forever, but it's long enough to save something. In the claims office I'd have nothing past 2031.

say: We have **five years** to put rules in place, so let's use them.
The union should bargain for **retraining money** in our contract.
think: Five years is long enough to be scared but maybe **not long enough** to change.
I'd probably **hope it away** for two years, then panic in year three.
do: Start the **electrician course** two nights a week next September.
Ask the union to get the **company to pay** part of the course.
Sell the car to reach **three months** of savings by 2030.
feel: **Heavy**, like walking toward a wall you can see coming.
S3.quote: I keep thinking I should be the kind of person who'd make a plan, and I'm not.
fieldNote: He knows his own pattern of **delay** and names it without being asked.
He needs an **outside push**, a paid course with a date, to act.
The robot gap makes a **trade** worth three extra years to him.

steps.text: Start the evening electrician course two nights a week next September
Ask the union to bargain for company-paid retraining
Sell the car and build three months of savings by 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair runway if the government actually uses it. I'd be the one at the union meeting asking for a transition plan with dates in it. People would probably shrug at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes it feel like a problem for later, which is exactly the danger with me. I'd be 37 when AGI comes. I'd have more experience, but more experience at a job that's going away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in claims for now but take the electrician course over two years instead of cramming it. I'd try to move from claims to the property repair side of the business, where you deal with builders and surveyors on site. And I'd want Lina and me to have a proper savings habit by 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. It's still my job going away, just on a longer fuse. At least with ten years I could do it at my own speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about kids or buying a home differently in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids around thirty, and I don't think we'd change that. But I wouldn't buy anywhere, I'd want to be able to move for work. Renting above the bakery suddenly sounds sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people at the top who'd see ten years coming and do nothing for staff. Our chief executive gets paid more in a month than my team does in a year. If they had a decade's warning and still dumped people, that's on them.

say: Ten years is a **fair runway** if the government actually uses it.
Every workplace needs a **transition plan** with real dates in it.
think: Ten years feels like **a problem for later**, which is the danger with me.
By 37 I'd have **more experience** in a job that's disappearing.
do: Take the **electrician course** slowly, over two years, while staying in claims.
Try to move into the **property repair** side, working with builders on site.
Build a **savings habit** with Lina before turning 30.
feel: **Calmer but not calm**, because the job still goes, just slower.
S4.quote: Our chief executive gets paid more in a month than my team does in a year.
fieldNote: The long timeline makes him **calmer** but he worries he'll waste it.
He looks for a **sideways move** inside the insurer toward on-site work.
He'd put any blame on **top management** who ignored a decade's warning.

steps.text: Take the electrician course part-time over two years
Apply for a role in the insurer's property repair team
Keep renting rather than buying so moving for work stays possible
Set up an automatic monthly savings transfer before turning 30

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. I'm all desk work, I've got no savings, and two years isn't enough for someone as slow to change as me. What would help is a paid course with a start date, and some kind of wage support while I retrain, so Lina isn't carrying us both.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who manage teams like mine. Everyone talks about the workers losing jobs, but somebody has to sit across the table and tell my team they're losing their jobs, and then I go home and check if I'm next.

headlineQuote: Somebody has to sit across the table and tell my team they're losing their jobs, and then I go home and check if I'm next.
portrait: Rafael is a 27-year-old **claims team leader** at a big insurer, renting with his partner Lina, a care home nurse.
He has **under a month** saved, lower pay for his role, and few similar office jobs in town.
He never uses AI, prints big claims out, and admits he's **slow to change**.
His answer to every picture is the **union**, plus a trade course he can barely afford.
He moves from anxious to **panicked** as AGI gets closer, and eases only with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his desk job goes fast and he has no savings to bridge it.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid retraining course** with a fixed start date.
**Wage support** while he retrains, so Lina doesn't carry the household alone.
